question.text: A <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>100</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi></math> of iron nail is hit by a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kg</mi></math> hammer striking at a velocity of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>60</mn><msup><mrow><mo> </mo><mi>ms</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>. What will be the rise in the temperature of the nail if one fourth of energy of the hammer goes into heating the nail ? [Specific heat capacity of iron <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>42</mn><msup><mi>Jg</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mmultiscripts><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mprescripts></mprescripts><none></none><mo>∘</mo></mmultiscripts><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>]

solution.text:
If we heat-up an object, then, the energy is used to either change the temperature of the body or to change the state of the body.
If it changes the temperature, then,

Q = mS∆T
where, Q is the heat given, m is the mass and ∆T is the change in temperature.

We know that a moving object has an energy in the form of kinetic energy, i.e.,
KE=12mv2

When that moving object strikes another object, it loses some energy which changes into the heat energy and this heat energy increases the temperature of the object.
Given a hammer of 1.5 kg is moving with 60 m s-1.
Kinetic energy =12mv2 = 12(1.5) (60)2 = 2700 J
One-fourth of kinetic energy changes into heat energy.
⇒   14(KE) = Heat energy
⇒   14(KE) = m(S)(∆T)
⇒   14(2700) =(100) (0.42) (∆T)
⇒   ∆T=16.07°C
